name: Capsaicin

lead: Capsaicin is the compound that makes chili peppers hot, and it is sold in capsules as a thermogenic and appetite supplement. People use it for a small metabolic and appetite boost during fat loss, and it comes up in discussions of lip plumping and facial leanness.

It activates the TRPV1 channel on sensory neurons, triggering sympathetic nervous system activity that raises heat production slightly, and it may affect fullness signalling and brown fat. Small human studies show modest rises in energy expenditure and fat oxidation; a 2014 meta-analysis found weak evidence that taking it before a meal might slightly reduce food intake.

paras: It is eaten as chili in food or taken as capsule supplements and chili extracts in thermogenic products, alongside diet and training. Effects are small and show up gradually.

Oral use can cause stomach pain, burning, nausea and diarrhoea, and may worsen reflux. Topical capsaicin burns and irritates, and contact with eyes or broken skin is painful. It is legal and unscheduled as food and supplement.

angle.text: Capsaicin from chili peppers gives a mild rise in energy expenditure and slightly lower appetite, which users add to fat-loss diets for a small contribution to leanness. Human studies show slight effects on energy use; the lip-plumping and facial-leanness claims come from users.

lead: Capsaicin (8-methyl-N-vanillyl-6-nonenamide) is the main pungent compound in chili peppers. It and related capsaicinoids are produced by plants of the genus Capsicum, likely as a deterrent to mammals and fungi, and it causes a burning sensation on contact with tissues in mammals [1].

In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding circles capsaicin is used for a body-composition goal: a leaner, more defined physique. Chili peppers, hot sauces and capsaicin or red-pepper-extract capsules are added to diets and to thermogenic fat-burner products on the premise that they raise energy expenditure and fat oxidation or reduce appetite, helping someone reach a lower body-fat level and so show more muscle and a sharper jawline and face [1][2][3]. Topical capsaicin creams are also used for joint and muscle aches, which can matter for people who train hard [1][4].

As a prescription topical, a high-concentration (8%) patch (Qutenza) was approved by the US FDA and in the European Union in 2009 for pain from post-herpetic neuralgia and has since been studied in diabetic neuropathy [1][5]. Research on capsaicin as a weight-management aid includes a 2023 meta-analysis of 15 randomised trials and several small controlled studies of energy expenditure and fat oxidation [2][3][6].
Capsaicin acts by binding the TRPV1 receptor on pain-sensing neurons, work that contributed to the 2021 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine awarded to David Julius and Ardem Patapoutian [1][7].

paras: Capsaicin is added to thermogenic fat-burner supplements and eaten in chilis in the belief that it increases heat production, fat oxidation and satiety [1]. Wikipedia's thermogenics article describes bodybuilders using such products to try to raise basal metabolic rate and reduce body fat, with caffeine and ephedrine the best-known components of classic stacks [8]. Researchers have measured capsaicin's effects under controlled conditions, including acute energy expenditure and fat oxidation and substrate oxidation after modest weight loss [2][3][6].

On T Nation's forum members describe capsaicin as one ingredient among several in cutting-phase routines. One long-running training log lists capsaicin alongside other supplements in a fat-loss stack [9], and a 2008 thread by a poster said he had been experimenting with red pepper extract and considered it a reasonable thing to add to a fat-loss phase, particularly in the later stages [10]. Another poster said spicy food helped with leg cramps while using clenbuterol [11].

Topical capsaicin relieves some neuropathic pain by desensitising nociceptor fibres. A 2017 review described moderate to substantial relief of post-herpetic, HIV and diabetic neuropathic pain with the 8% preparation versus a 0.4% control, with limited quality of evidence, and the 12-week phase III trial in painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy found a larger pain reduction with the 8% patch than placebo (about 27 percent versus 21 percent) [1][5]. Reviews of neuropathic pain treatment and of painful diabetic neuropathy discuss capsaicin among the options [12][13][14]. Wikipedia notes insufficient evidence for itch (pruritus) and low-quality evidence that oral capsaicin may modestly lower LDL cholesterol [1].

Over-the-counter capsaicin creams carry labelling for temporary relief of minor aches and pains of muscles and joints from backache, arthritis, strains and sprains. Labels advise external use only, testing on a small area first, avoiding eyes, lips and mucous membranes, not using on wounds or damaged skin, and not applying heat to the treated area; they warn that a burning sensation is expected and generally fades with regular use [4]. A lifter on T Nation reported applying capsaicin cream to a sore elbow and said it helped [15].

Capsaicin gives the heat in chili powder, hot sauces and curries, and capsaicinoids are the active ingredients in pepper sprays and in repellents for mammals such as deer and rabbits [1][16]. Law-enforcement sprays are often rated at 500,000 to 2,000,000 Scoville heat units, a measure Wikipedia calls unreliable for sprays [16]. Capsaicin is banned in equestrian sports, and four horses were disqualified after testing positive at the 2008 Olympic show jumping events [1].

sections.h: Effectiveness for weight and body composition
paras: A 2023 British Journal of Nutrition meta-analysis pooled 15 randomised trials with 762 overweight or obese adults. Capsaicin supplementation was associated with a small reduction in body weight (about 0.5 kg), BMI (about 0.25 kg/m2) and waist circumference (about 1.1 cm), with no significant change in waist-to-hip ratio; the authors described the effects as fairly small and called for more prospective studies [2].

A 2013 PLOS ONE study used a single-blind crossover design in which 15 healthy adults spent four 36-hour stays in a respiration chamber, eating either full or reduced energy with or without capsaicin (about 2.56 mg per meal from red chili). In the reduced-energy condition, capsaicin was associated with higher fat oxidation and with the avoidance of the drop in some energy expenditure measures seen with calorie restriction alone; blood pressure did not differ significantly. The study was funded by a spice company and the authors noted the small sample [3]. An earlier trial examined substrate oxidation and weight maintenance after modest weight loss [6].

Wikipedia reports that, as of 2007, no evidence had shown weight loss to be directly correlated with ingesting capsaicin; that well-designed research has been hampered because the pungency of the doses used prevented participants from complying; and that a 2014 meta-analysis found weak evidence that taking it before a meal might slightly reduce food intake and shift preference toward carbohydrates [1].

Christian Friedrich Bucholz first extracted it in impure form in 1816, and Rudolf Buchheim (1873) and Endre Hogyes (1878) attributed the burning feeling to the substance [1]. Wikipedia adds that J. C. Thresh obtained it in almost pure form in the 1870s and that its structure and synthesis were worked out in the 1910s and 1930s [1]. The first pesticide registered by the US Department of Agriculture containing only capsaicin was approved in 1962 [1].

Pure capsaicin is a hydrophobic, crystalline white solid that dissolves well in alcohol and poorly in water. The common capsaicinoids are capsaicin (about 69 percent of the mix), dihydrocapsaicin (about 22 percent) and nordihydrocapsaicin (about 7 percent) [1]. Pungency is measured in Scoville heat units; capsaicin itself rates about 16,000,000 [1]. It is concentrated in the placental tissue that holds the seeds. Birds lack a sensitive capsaicin receptor and disperse the seeds, which fits the idea that the compound deters mammals [1]. Capsinoids are related non-pungent compounds found in paprika [1].

Capsaicin binds the TRPV1 ion channel on nociceptors, which is also activated by heat above about 43 degrees C and by acid, causing cation influx, depolarisation and sensations of burning. Prolonged activation leads to desensitisation or defunctionalisation of the fibres, which underlies its use as an analgesic [1][17][18][19][7]. TRPV1 was cloned in 1997 by David Julius's group as a heat-activated ion channel in the pain pathway, and mice lacking it showed impaired pain sensation [20][21][7]. Wikipedia notes that TRPV1 also appears to help regulate body temperature: antagonists of the channel often raise body temperature, and one was dropped from clinical trials because of hyperthermia [7].

Oral capsaicin is efficiently absorbed from the gut (85 percent in rats) but undergoes extensive first-pass liver metabolism. In human volunteers who ingested a Capsicum extract, the blood half-life was about 25 minutes with peak levels at 45 minutes. Topical capsaicin reaches the stratum corneum within a minute [1].

Capsaicin is a strong irritant of skin, eyes and airways. Ingesting large amounts can cause nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain and burning diarrhea, and eye exposure causes intense tearing and pain; Wikipedia also reports that ingestion of very high quantities can be fatal, particularly in people with heart problems, and that myocardial infarction has been reported after ingesting capsaicin capsules [1]. The reported LD50 in mice is 47.2 mg/kg [1]. Pepper exposures are among the most common plant-related calls to poison centres [1]. Plain water is ineffective at removing it from skin; alcohol dissolves it, and cold milk may relieve burning after ingestion [1]. Wikipedia's pepper spray article reports that eye irritation from sprays can persist for up to 24 hours and that deaths have been linked to police use of sprays, with causes debated [16].

Capsaicin is legal and unscheduled as a food ingredient and supplement. The 8% Qutenza patch is prescription-only in the United States, approved by the FDA in 2009 and authorised in the European Union [1]. Civilian pepper spray is banned in the UK, Mexico and Hong Kong, restricted in many European countries and legal with limits in all 50 US states [16].

For weight: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials examined capsaicin intake in overweight and obese subjects, a PLOS ONE study measured the acute effects of capsaicin on energy expenditure and fat oxidation, and an earlier trial examined substrate oxidation and weight maintenance after modest weight loss [2][3][6]. For pain: the 8% patch trial enrolled 369 patients, with a shorter median time to response (19 versus 72 days) and modest improvements in sleep interference; application-site reactions were the main adverse events [5]. Other registered trials examine the patch in cancer-related neuropathic pain, post-surgical neuropathic pain, coccygodynia and amputation [22][23][24]. A 2024 randomized trial tested topical capsaicin for delayed chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting, and a 2015 trial tested its use in cough reduction [25][26]. Reviews of burning mouth syndrome treatment also include capsaicin [27].

lore.intro: On bodybuilding forums capsaicin appears mainly as a small cutting-phase add-on in diet and supplement stacks, and as a topical for sore joints [10][9][15].
